name: Kamwe
sweep_summary: Kamwe (Higi) is not in the catalog. Both sweep items - Barreteau 1983 'Phonémique et prosodie en higi' and Mohrlang 1971 'Vectors, prosodies, and Higi vowels' - use 'prosody' in the Firthian sense (word/syllable-level labialisation, palatalisation, prenasalisation conditioning vowels and consonants), not word stress; two open secondary sources that summarise them (Gravina 2014 LOT thesis pp.74-75, 168-169; Wolff 2025 LangSci ch.7 pp.267-275, 293) report no stress claim and show Higi forms with tone marks. Neither item is online: SIL archives list all three Mohrlang works (1971 article, 1972 'Higi phonology', 1974 'Higi' in Ten Nigerian tone systems) as 'Not Available Online'; the Buske 1983 volume and the 1974 tone volume are HathiTrust search-only (bot-challenged), Google Books no-view; Journal of African Languages 10 not found in any digital library; IRD Horizon search endpoint unusable; No first-hand statement on Kamwe word stress was read (best_new_statement found=false). Acquisition priority: Mohrlang 1972 Higi phonology (106 pp., Harvard microfiche TOZ Microfiche L.SOC. 120.Tx. 8.5.12.1 (2)) high; Barreteau 1983 (28 pp.) and Mohrlang 1974 tone sketch medium; Mohrlang 1971 low. fetched sources material and

new_statements.quote: In general, stress is predictable and seems to be a feature of vowel length. In a sequence of similar vowels, however, high tone syllables tend to have more stress than low tone syllables.[1] [fn. 1:] It is interesting to note than in an analysis of Kapsiki, a Higi dialect in North Cameroun, David Smith states that it would be possible to postulate that "Kapsiki is a tone language in the process of changing to a stress-intonation-type language". [...] "This is realised as a raising of pitch and an increase in intensity on the ultima or penult of the intonation phrase and can be termed primary stress." He goes on to describe a type of secondary stress which occurs with non-final high tones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Higi is a tone language (two level tonemes H and L plus a LH glide toneme; pitch functions at the syllable and pause-group levels). Stress is not contrastive: it is predictable and is essentially a by-product of vowel length (long vowels sound stressed); where vowels are alike, high-tone syllables carry more stress than low-tone syllables. No positional word-stress rule is given for Higi itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated for Higi. The footnote reports Smith 1969 on Kapsiki (a Cameroonian 'Higi dialect' = Psikye): primary stress on the ultima or penult of the intonation phrase, plus a secondary stress on non-final high tones.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the tone-conditioned tendency ('high tone syllables tend to have more stress').
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable-level statement (stress as correlate of vowel length and tone); the Kapsiki material in the footnote is phrase-level (intonation phrase). Section 9.3 immediately before deals with intonational raising of pitch (extra-high on question words). Text reached only through Google Books snippet windows (about 40 overlapping windows, all mutually consistent); scanned artefacts possible ('than' for 'that', 'Kapsikit' for 'Kapsiki' + footnote mark); page number inferred, not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Mohrlang's 'Higi' is Kamwe of the Michika area, Nigeria: the chapter intro (snippet) says 'Higi language is a Chadic language comprising several dialects spoken by the Kamwe people, as they prefer to call themselves, who live around Michika'; Ruhlen 1976 labels his data 'HIGI (Nkafa) (Mohrlang 1972)', i.e. the Nkafa dialect. The footnote's Kapsiki ('a Higi dialect in North Cameroun', Smith 1969) is Psikye [psik1239] in Glottolog, a separate language; its phrase-penult/ultima stress statement must not be attributed to kamw1239.

sources.quote: p.267: 'This, however, led to postulating extremely rich inventories for individual Central Chadic languages, e.g. almost 80 consonantal phonemes for Bura (Margi: Hoffmann 1987) and more than 90 for Higi (Higi: Barreteau 1983). The idea of treating labialisation, palatalisation, prenasalisation, and combinations of these as "prosodies" allowed for the considerable reduction of the consonantal inventories.' ... 'Roger Mohrlang and James Hoskison took notice and used the approach for their own work on Higi (Mohrlang 1971, 1972)'.
sources.note: Discusses Hoffmann 1965, Mohrlang 1971/1972 and Barreteau 1983 analyses of Higi vowels/prosodies (Table 6); grep for stress/accent in the Higi passages finds nothing.
